## `src/lib/app-update.ts`

Deciding what to tell someone about updates. Shared by the server
(/api/version) and the browser (UpdateManager); pure, so
scripts/check-updates.ts can exercise it.

Two kinds of update:
  - the site: every phone and browser runs the live site, so a new deploy
    only needs the page reloaded. A page knows its own build id
    (NEXT_PUBLIC_BUILD_ID) and compares it with the server's;
  - the phone app itself (the Android APK or the iPhone app), which needs
    installing. Only needed when something native changed, such as the
    shift tracker. An admin can set the lowest build still allowed.

Exports: `ReleaseNote`, `VersionInfo`, `UpdateLevel`, `UpdateState`, `buildNumber`, `decideUpdate`, `NOTES_FRESH_DAYS`, `shouldShowNotes`, `InstallStatus`, `installStatus`

## `src/lib/client-ip.ts`

The address a request came from, as the app's own proxy saw it.

X-Forwarded-For is a list each proxy appends to, so anything a client
writes in it comes first and the entries the proxies add come last. The
first entry is therefore whatever the caller chose to put there. This
reads from the end instead, skipping the proxies Xtend sits behind:

  TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS=1  Nginx or Caddy on the VPS, or Vercel (default)
  TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS=2  Cloudflare in front of Nginx, and so on

Without the header (a request straight to Node), X-Real-IP, which Nginx
sets from the connection itself.

Exports: `requestIp`

## `src/lib/geocode.ts`

Resolving "where is this person standing" into something a human reads as
a place: "Justrite Superstore Bariga, 56/58 Jagun Molu St, Bariga, Lagos".

Three sources, best first:

 1. The assigned outlet, when the fix is inside its geofence. If someone
    is standing in their own store, the store's own record is the most
    accurate answer there is, and it costs no API call.
 2. Google — Places (New) for the business name, Geocoding for the street
    address. This is the only source that reliably names Nigerian retail
    premises, and it is what produces the format above. Needs
    GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY with "Places API (New)" and "Geocoding API"
    enabled on the project.
 3. OpenStreetMap — Nominatim for the address, Overpass for a named
    business within 80 m. Free and needs no key, but Nigerian POI
    coverage is thin, so it often names the street rather than the shop.

Exports: `PlaceSource`, `ResolvedPlace`, `OutletAnchor`, `resolvePlace`, `LocatedPlace`, `locateAddress`

## `src/lib/integrity-signals.ts`

The manipulation checks that need more than the GPS columns: the request
IP, the phone's time zone, and the GPS fix's extra fields. Pure and
side-effect free. The caller records whatever comes back through the
flag_own_integrity() RPC.

Every check is deliberately forgiving. A Nigerian marketer on a mobile
network can carry a carrier IP that geolocates a city or two away, so the
distance threshold is generous and a mobile IP softens it further. The aim
is to catch someone sitting at home behind a VPN with a fake GPS pin, not
to punish a weak signal.

Exports: `SignalKind`, `Signal`, `EvaluateInput`, `EvaluateResult`, `evaluateLocationIntegrity`

## `src/lib/ip-geo.ts`

IP geolocation for the VPN / location-manipulation checks.

Free and keyless by default: ip-api.com returns a lat/lng, a country, and
crucially a proxy / hosting flag that marks VPN and datacentre IPs, with no
sign-up (45 requests a minute, which is far above Xtend's clock-in rate).
Swap the provider by pointing IP_GEO_URL at another HTTPS JSON endpoint that
uses the same field names, set IP_API_KEY to use ip-api's paid HTTPS
endpoint, or set IP_GEO_DISABLED=1 to turn the lookup off.

When the lookup cannot run (no network, a private IP, the rate limit), the
caller simply gets null and the IP-based checks are skipped for that event.
A clock-in is never blocked by this.

Exports: `IpGeo`, `clientIp`, `lookupIp`

printed photo, or too poor to show anything? Only a clear problem is a
rejection; anything uncertain passes, because blocking an honest clock-in
is worse than letting a doubtful one through to the integrity flags.

or of a printed photo), and an honest photo should never fail here.

## `src/lib/push-native.ts`

Push to the Xtend Android and iOS apps (mobile/). Web push does not reach
an app, so each phone's own service is used:

  Android — Firebase Cloud Messaging, HTTP v1.
    FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT: the service account key JSON from the
    Firebase console (Project settings → Service accounts).
  iOS — Apple Push Notification service, HTTP/2 with a token key.
    APNS_KEY (the .p8 file's contents), APNS_KEY_ID, APNS_TEAM_ID,
    APNS_BUNDLE_ID (default ng.xpelbeauty.xtend), APNS_SANDBOX=true for
    builds run from Xcode.

A device is stored in push_subscriptions with an endpoint of
"native-fcm:<token>" or "native-apns:<token>" (migration 033).

Exports: `NATIVE_PREFIX`, `isNativeEndpoint`, `NativeOutcome`, `sendNative`, `nativePushConfigured`

## `src/lib/support-assistant.ts`

The AI that answers a field member's support message.

It reads the whole thread, replies in plain language to what it can handle
on its own (how the app works, what a status means, what to do next), and
when the issue needs a person, or it is not sure, it says so briefly and
escalates the thread to the office. It never changes an account, a store
allocation, a password or a record: those are exactly what it escalates.

Runs with the service-role client, because it writes the AI's reply and,
on escalation, pushes to the office. It is called from the support routes
after the member's message is saved.

## `src/components/field/use-dashboard-refresh.ts`

Keep the phone dashboard in step with the backend.

The fast path is Supabase realtime Broadcast: a database trigger sends one
lightweight event to the member's own private topic `field:<uid>` whenever
their attendance, store visit, support message or notification changes
(migration 0058). The event carries only { table, op }; the screen re-fetches
on it and that fetch goes through RLS, so the socket never carries row data.
Broadcast replaces Postgres Changes here because it does not run RLS per
subscriber per change, so the same Supabase compute holds far more
connections — the thing that caps how many staff can be on shift at once.

Behind it sits a slow poll as a safety net for anything realtime can miss:
a dropped socket, or a value the server computes only when the page is
read. It is far slower than the old 15s poll, because realtime now does the
work that used to need constant refreshing, which also makes the app feel
quicker and spares the battery and data.

At scale (thousands of field staff on shift at once) three things matter:
  - Only on-shift members hold a socket (see below); everyone else polls.
  - NEXT_PUBLIC_REALTIME_DISABLED=1 turns realtime off fleet-wide and lets
    everyone ride the poll instead — a safe release valve if the socket
    count is still the thing falling over.
  - If every client polled on the same 45s boundary the backend would see a
    spike every 45s instead of steady traffic, so the poll is jittered per
    client to spread that load out.

Exports: `useDashboardRefresh`

## `src/middleware.ts`

Refreshes the Supabase session cookie on every navigation so field staff
are not logged out mid-shift, and keeps unauthenticated users off the app.
Role enforcement itself lives in Postgres; this is only routing.

It must live in src/, beside app/: Next.js ignores a middleware file at
the project root when the app is under src/.

Exports: `middleware`, `config`

## `public/sw.js`

Xtend service worker.
Deliberately small. The app shell is cached so a cold start on 3G is not a
white screen, and navigations fall back to /offline when the network is
gone. Writes are NOT replayed here: they live in the IndexedDB outbox and
are flushed by the page, which owns the auth session.
